The [Decimal to BCD Converter](/decimal-to-bcd-converter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Convert a decimal number to Binary-Coded Decimal — each digit as 4 bits. Enter your decimal number (whole number) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Convert a decimal number to Binary-Coded Decimal (BCD): each decimal digit is written as its own 4-bit binary group, instead of converting the whole number to binary at once. 93 becomes 1001 0011 — 9 as 1001 and 3 as 0011 — which is not the same as 93 in plain binary (1011101). BCD is how many digital clocks, calculators and old mainframes stored numbers, because it keeps decimal digits intact and makes decimal arithmetic and seven-segment displays straightforward.

## How to use the Decimal to BCD Converter

Start by typing or pasting your decimal number (whole number). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Enter a whole non-negative decimal number.
2. Read the BCD groups — one 4-bit group per decimal digit.
3. The packed hex line shows the same digits squeezed into bytes.

## Formula

Write each decimal digit d as a 4-bit binary number (d in binary, padded to 4 bits) and join the groups. 0–9 map to 0000–1001; the codes 1010–1111 are unused in BCD.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Decimal to BCD Converter](/decimal-to-bcd-converter) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. 93 in BCD is 1001 0011: the digit 9 is 1001 and the digit 3 is 0011. Packed together that is 0x93. Plain binary 93 would be 1011101 — a different number of bits and a different value if read as BCD. Try the same figures in the [Decimal to BCD Converter](/decimal-to-bcd-converter) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Decimal number (whole number): 93), the [Decimal to BCD Converter](/decimal-to-bcd-converter) returns BCD (4 bits per digit): 1001 0011, Packed BCD (hex): 0x93, Digits: 9 → 1001, 3 → 0011, Digit count: 2. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. ## BCD vs plain binary

In plain binary, 93 is 1011101 — seven bits for the whole number. In BCD, 93 is 1001 0011 — eight bits, but each group of four is a decimal digit you can read directly. BCD wastes bits (the codes 1010–1111 are never used) and needs more storage, but it makes decimal arithmetic exact: adding 0.1 ten times in BCD gives exactly 1.0, where binary floating point gives 0.9999999999999999.

## Where BCD is still used

BCD survives wherever decimal digits must be exact or displayed directly: real-time clock chips, seven-segment displays, financial and accounting systems that cannot tolerate binary rounding, and the packed-decimal format of IBM mainframes. It is also a staple of electronics courses, because it is the clearest bridge between the decimal numbers humans use and the binary numbers machines use.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Read BCD in groups of four bits — each group is one decimal digit, 0–9.
- 1010–1111 never appear in valid BCD; if you see them, the data is not BCD.
- BCD is not the same as binary: 93 is 1011101 in binary but 1001 0011 in BCD.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is BCD?

Binary-Coded Decimal: a way of writing decimal numbers in binary where each decimal digit gets its own 4-bit group. 93 becomes 1001 0011 instead of the plain binary 1011101. Try it with your own numbers in the [Decimal to BCD Converter](/decimal-to-bcd-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why use BCD instead of binary?

Because it keeps decimal digits exact. Decimal arithmetic in BCD has no binary rounding error, and each digit maps directly onto a seven-segment display — useful in clocks, calculators and financial systems. Try it with your own numbers in the [Decimal to BCD Converter](/decimal-to-bcd-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How many bits does a BCD digit need?

Four bits per digit, holding 0–9. The six codes 1010–1111 are unused, which is why BCD takes more space than plain binary. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.

### What formula does the Decimal to BCD Converter use?

Write each decimal digit d as a 4-bit binary number (d in binary, padded to 4 bits) and join the groups. 0–9 map to 0000–1001; the codes 1010–1111 are unused in BCD.
